section.title: Miracles and the Plentiful Harvest
section.sectionRationale: The miracle collection reaches its climax and turns toward mission. Jesus raises a dead girl and heals a woman who touches His cloak, opens the eyes of two who hail Him Son of David, and frees a mute man, dividing the crowds from the hardening Pharisees. Then, moved with compassion for the shepherdless crowds, He calls His disciples to pray for workers for the plentiful harvest.
section.thesis: The Son of David displays His authority over disease, death, and demons, and reveals the compassion of the true Shepherd for harassed and helpless crowds, so that the mounting miracles both provoke a decisive division and drive His people to pray for laborers for a plentiful harvest.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the dead girl raised and the bleeding woman healed; two blind men receive sight; a mute demoniac is freed as the Pharisees blaspheme; and Jesus' compassion moves Him to call for workers for the harvest.

verses.text: While Jesus was saying these things, a synagogue leader came and knelt before Him. “My daughter has just died,” he said. “But come and place Your hand on her, and she will live.”
So Jesus got up and went with him, along with His disciples.
Suddenly a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years came up behind Him and touched the fringe of His cloak.
She said to herself, “If only I touch His cloak, I will be healed.”
Jesus turned and saw her. “Take courage, daughter,” He said, “your {{pistis|faith}} has healed you.” And the woman was healed from that very hour.
When Jesus entered the house of the synagogue leader, He saw the flute players and the noisy crowd.
“Go away,” He told them. “The girl is not dead, but asleep.” And they laughed at Him.
After the crowd had been put outside, Jesus went in and took the girl by the hand, and she got up.
And the news about this spread throughout that region.

units.label: Two blind men, Son of David

verses.text: As Jesus went on from there, two blind men followed Him, crying out, “Have mercy on us, {{huiosdavid|Son of David}}!”
After Jesus had entered the house, the blind men came to Him. “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” He asked. “Yes, Lord,” they answered.
Then He touched their eyes and said, “According to your faith will it be done to you.”
And their eyes were opened. Jesus warned them sternly, “See that no one finds out about this!”
But they went out and spread the news about Him throughout the land.

units.label: The mute man and the charge

verses.text: As they were leaving, a demon-possessed man who was mute was brought to Jesus.
And when the demon had been driven out, the man began to speak. The crowds were amazed and said, “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel!”
But the Pharisees said, “It is by the prince of demons that He drives out demons.”
Jesus went through all the towns and villages, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness.
When He saw the crowds, He was moved with {{splanchnizomai|compassion}} for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.
Then He said to His disciples, “The {{therismos|harvest}} is plentiful, but the workers are few.
Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest.”

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust, reliance. The bleeding woman and the blind men receive from Jesus through faith; her trust reaches out to touch His cloak, and He tells her that faith has made her well, showing that healing comes through believing dependence on Him.

huiosdavid.gloss: Son of David, the royal messianic title. The blind men, who cannot see, perceive what many miss: that Jesus is the promised King of David's line. Matthew uses the title to press Jesus' identity as the Messiah.

splanchnizomai.gloss: To be moved with compassion in one's inmost being, from the word for the gut or heart. Jesus feels the crowds' plight deep within; His mercy is not distant pity but a visceral, shepherd's love for the harassed and helpless.

therismos.gloss: Harvest, the reaping of a ripe crop, often an image of the ingathering of people at the end of the age. The plentiful harvest is the multitude ready to be gathered into the kingdom; the shortage is of workers to reap it.

basic.context: A synagogue leader begs Jesus to raise his just-dead daughter. On the way, a woman sick with bleeding for twelve years touches His cloak in faith and is healed. Jesus reaches the house, dismisses the mourners, and raises the girl by the hand. Two blind men call Him Son of David and receive sight; a mute demoniac is freed and speaks. The crowds marvel while the Pharisees blaspheme. Seeing the shepherdless crowds, Jesus is moved with compassion and calls for harvest workers.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this cluster as the peak of the miracle section, showing Jesus' authority over the last enemies: disease, death, and demons. Notice the two responses that now sharpen, the crowds' amazement and the Pharisees' hardened charge. The closing verses turn from miracle to mission: the same compassion that healed individuals now looks on the crowds and calls for laborers.
basic.originalLanguages: The bleeding woman and the blind men receive through faith, a trusting dependence on Jesus. The blind hail Him Son of David, seeing His messianic identity though they cannot see. Jesus is moved with compassion, a gut-deep mercy, for the shepherdless crowds. And He speaks of a plentiful harvest, a ripe multitude ready to be gathered, needing workers.
basic.typology: The shepherdless crowds recall Israel's longing for the true Shepherd God promised to send. Jesus raising the dead girl anticipates His power over death itself, fulfilled in His resurrection. And the harvest imagery draws on the prophetic vision of God gathering His people at the end of the age.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Son of David, the Messiah, whose touch heals and whose word raises the dead. He is the compassionate Shepherd Israel lacked, moved to His core by the crowds' plight. He is Lord over death, calling it mere sleep, and Lord of the harvest, though here He tells His disciples to ask the Lord of the harvest for workers, drawing them into His mission.
basic.god: God's compassion is embodied in Jesus, who feels the crowds' helplessness and acts. He is the Lord of the harvest to whom we must pray for workers. He honors faith, whether a trembling touch or a blind man's cry, and He is sovereign over disease, death, and the demonic, none of which can withstand His Son.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 27 and Ezekiel 34 lament sheep without a shepherd and promise God's own shepherding. John 11 shows Jesus as the resurrection and the life. Matthew 20 repeats the Son of David cry from blind men. And Luke 10 sends out workers into the harvest.
basic.oneStory: The miracles crest here as Jesus conquers disease, death, and demons, revealing Himself as the Son of David and the compassionate Shepherd. But the crowds are harassed and helpless, and His mercy turns toward mission. The story pivots from what the King does alone to what He will send His people to do, praying for and becoming workers in a harvest that is ripe and vast.

context.literary:
Matthew 8 and 9 are built as a collection of ten mighty works, arranged in three groups of three with teaching and discipleship scenes threaded between them. This passage carries the last of the ten and gathers the whole collection into one summary. The summary in verse 35 repeats the wording of Matthew 4:23 almost exactly, teaching, preaching and healing, so that chapters 5 to 9 stand between two matching brackets: the Sermon on the Mount, the word of the Messiah, and the miracles, the deeds of the Messiah. Matthew has shown the King in speech and in action, and now he shows what the King sees.

The opening scene is a sandwich, a literary device Mark uses freely and Matthew keeps in compressed form. The request of the synagogue leader in verse 18 is interrupted by the woman in verses 20 to 22, and the story of the girl resumes in verse 23. The two stories cross-light each other. One suffers twelve years; the other has lived twelve years. One is an outcast approaching in secret; the other belongs to a respected family and is approached in public. Both are called daughter or girl, both are touched, and in both Jesus crosses a boundary of uncleanness. Matthew trims the narrative so that these links stand clear.

The two scenes of verses 27 to 34 are a matched pair as well. Both begin with an affliction, blindness and muteness, and both end with the news running out, in verse 31 with the healed men disobeying a command to silence and in verse 33 with the crowds saying nothing like this was seen in Israel. They close with the reply of the Pharisees, which is the first open charge against Jesus in this gospel that He works by the prince of demons.

Then the camera pulls back. After four scenes of single persons, verse 36 turns to the crowds, and the movement of the whole passage is from the one to the many: one dead girl, one woman, two men, one mute man, then all the towns and villages. The final saying about the harvest is the hinge to chapter 10, where the same verb and the same twelve who are told to pray for workers become the workers themselves.
context.historical:
The synagogue leader was a lay officer who oversaw the building and the order of the service, usually a man of standing in a Galilean town. To kneel before a wandering teacher with a sick child at home, in front of onlookers, shows desperation that overrides dignity. His request is also unusually bold. The Old Testament knows of a few raisings, 1 Kings 17:17-24 and 2 Kings 4:32-35, and in each the prophet strains and prays over the child. The father asks for something Jesus has not yet done in Matthew, and he asks only for a hand laid on her.

The woman's condition falls under Leviticus 15:25-27. A long discharge of blood made her unclean, and the uncleanness spread by contact to anything she touched or sat on. Twelve years of this meant twelve years of isolation from worship, from ordinary table fellowship and very likely from marriage. She reaches for the fringe of His cloak. Israelite men wore tassels on the corners of their garments as a reminder to keep the commandments, Numbers 15:37-39, and she takes hold of that sign of the law's authority, hoping for healing without being seen. In Matthew 14:36 crowds ask to touch the same fringe and are made well.

Mourning at a death began at once. Even a modest household was expected to engage flute players and wailers, and Matthew's flute players and noisy crowd are already in place when Jesus arrives, which shows how final the household judged the death to be. Their laughter in verse 24 is the laughter of people who know what death looks like.

Son of David was a title heavy with hope. It recalled the promise of an heir whose throne would last forever, 2 Samuel 7:12-16, and the prophets who spoke of a coming shepherd king from David's line, Ezekiel 34:23. Under Roman rule, to hail a man in the street as Son of David was politically dangerous, which may explain why Jesus quiets the two men in verse 30 and why He waits to show His royal identity openly. The charge in verse 34 also has a setting. Exorcism was practised in Jewish circles of the day, so the Pharisees cannot deny that the demon left. They can only attack the source of the power.
context.canonical:
The great background of this passage is the biblical image of the shepherd, and Matthew reaches for it in verse 36 with an almost exact echo of Numbers 27:17, where Moses prays that the congregation not be like sheep without a shepherd, and of 1 Kings 22:17, where Micaiah sees Israel scattered on the hills. Both texts name a gap in leadership. Ezekiel 34 explains why the gap exists: the shepherds fed themselves and did not strengthen the weak, heal the sick or search for the lost, Ezekiel 34:2-6. The remedy comes in the same chapter as a promise that the LORD Himself will seek the lost, bind up the broken and strengthen the weak, Ezekiel 34:16, and then that He will appoint one shepherd, His servant David, Ezekiel 34:23. Verse 27's Son of David and verse 36's Shepherd are therefore one claim looked at from two sides.

The miracle list answers Isaiah 35:5-6, where the eyes of the blind are opened and the mute tongue shouts for joy, and Jesus will say so to John in Matthew 11:5. Matthew himself explains the healings in 8:17 with Isaiah 53:4. The girl and the woman, taken together, point to the Lord who heals and raises, as in the later Gospels the daughter of Jairus joins the widow's son in Luke 7:11-17 and Lazarus in John 11 as signs of the final resurrection.

The harvest has two faces in the Bible. In the prophets it can be the harvest of judgment, Joel 3:13, and John the Baptist used the picture of wheat gathered and chaff burned, Matthew 3:12. It can also be the gathering of the scattered, Isaiah 27:12. Jesus uses it here in the second sense, as the ingathering of people ready to be reached. In John 4:35 He tells the disciples to lift their eyes and see fields ripe for harvest, and Luke 10:2 repeats this saying nearly word for word when the seventy are sent. The prayer of verse 38 becomes the church's ongoing prayer for mission, answered in Acts 13:1-3, where the Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew arranges this passage to answer a question his readers will be asked in every generation: who is this Jesus, and what is to be done about Him? He lets the evidence pile up, a dead child, a woman who was shut out, men who cannot see yet name Him, a man who cannot speak, and then he records the two verdicts. The crowds are amazed but do not commit; the leaders explain it away. Matthew wants his readers to see that signs by themselves do not compel faith, and that the only sound response is the one the suffering gave, a plain, trusting approach to Jesus.

He also wants the compassion of Jesus to be the key to the whole collection. The miracles are not displays of power for its own sake. Verse 36 tells us why Jesus does what He does: He sees people as sheep with no one tending them. A reader who has felt overlooked, or a church tempted to treat people as numbers, is meant to see the Messiah's eyes in verse 36.

Finally, Matthew wants his readers to understand that the compassion of Jesus has a plan for how it spreads. The disciples are not told to feel sorry for the crowds; they are told to pray, and by praying they will find themselves sent. The author is preparing the ground for chapter 10 and for the church's mission, so that the reader finishes this passage at the edge of obedience rather than at rest after a miracle.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The raising of a dead child, the healing at a touch and the opening of blind eyes are recorded as acts of the Messiah at a pivotal moment in the story. They show who He is; they are not a pattern that promises the same result for every request today. Nor does the passage turn the woman's secret touch into a technique. Jesus does not say that touching His clothing heals; He says her faith has healed her, and Matthew never treats the fringe as a charm.

What does carry over as prescription is narrower and clearer. First, the way the needy come to Jesus is the way anyone may come: they ask, they trust, and they say plainly what they want. Second, His reply to the blind men, that it will be done according to their faith, is not a rule that faith earns the miracle, but a statement that He answers real trust. Third, verses 37 and 38 are a direct command with a plain application. The prayer for workers is for every disciple to pray, and a prayer that is honest will be followed by willingness. The passage does not command that we raise the dead; it commands that we ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers, and we should not be surprised if we are among them.

debates.question: What did Jesus mean when He said the dead girl was only asleep?

views.label: She was truly dead; sleep expresses hope of resurrection
views.case: The father says she has just died and mourners are already gathered; Jesus calls death sleep because in His presence it is temporary and reversible, as sleep is, pointing to His power over death.

views.label: A gentle way of describing what He would undo
views.case: Whether or not one presses the medical question, Jesus deliberately reframes death as sleep to declare that, for Him, raising her is as simple as waking a sleeper, which the mockers cannot grasp.

debates.bearing: Both affirm Jesus' mastery over death: what terrifies humanity He treats as sleep, foreshadowing His own resurrection and the raising of His people.

debates.question: Why did the Pharisees attribute Jesus' exorcism to the prince of demons?

views.label: A hardening refusal to accept the obvious
views.case: Unable to deny the miracle, they explain it away with a slander, revealing hearts so set against Jesus that even undeniable good is credited to evil; their opposition is now deliberate.

views.label: A defense of their threatened authority
views.case: Jesus' popularity and power endangered their standing, so they attacked His source rather than His works, choosing to discredit Him rather than submit to what God was plainly doing.

debates.bearing: Both show the deepening division: the same deeds that move the crowds to wonder harden the leaders, a charge Jesus will confront directly in chapter 12.

debates.question: Why did Jesus tell the healed blind men to tell no one, and why did they speak anyway?

views.label: He guarded against a political misreading
views.case: The men had just called Him Son of David. In a land under Rome, news of a healed multitude following a claimed heir of David could provoke a premature crowd movement or a crackdown. Silence kept His mission on the road to the cross that He intended.

views.label: He wanted faith shaped by His teaching, not by rumour
views.case: Matthew shows crowds who were amazed but not changed. Jesus resists a fame built on wonders alone, and the demand for silence presses the hearers toward the longer road of following Him.

debates.bearing: Either way, the sternness of the warning in verse 30 and the spreading news of verse 31 show a tension Matthew leaves unresolved: gratitude cannot stay quiet, yet Jesus will be known on His own terms, as the Servant who comes by suffering before He comes in glory.

study.originalLanguages:
Matthew 9:22 uses a word that English renders as healing but that is wider in Greek. Jesus says the woman's faith has sesoken her, from sozo, to save, rescue or make whole. The woman in verse 21 says to herself that she will be sothesomai, the same verb, so that her own hope and His verdict use the same word, and Matthew adds that she was healed from that very hour. The verb is used elsewhere for physical rescue, as when Peter cries out in the sea in Matthew 14:30, and for the rescue of the soul, Matthew 1:21. The word lets the reader hear that the touch and the forgiveness of sins belong to one saving ministry, even though the story here is bodily.

Jesus' address to her, tharsei, is a short imperative meaning take courage or be of good cheer. It is the same word He spoke to the paralysed man in verse 2 of this chapter and to the frightened disciples on the sea in Matthew 14:27. In each case the word stands where fear is strongest, and in each case it is followed by a reason: your sins are forgiven, it is I, your faith has made you well. The word is a command to the heart that rests on a person, not on a mood.

In verse 24 Jesus says the girl katheudei, sleeps. The verb is an ordinary one for sleep, but the Bible also uses it of the dead, 1 Thessalonians 4:13-14, and John 11:11-14 shows Jesus using the same picture of Lazarus and then explaining that He meant death. The raising in verse 25 uses egeiro, to rouse or raise, the verb that will be used again and again of the resurrection of Jesus, as in Matthew 28:6. The girl rises, and the language lines up with the Easter story that follows.

The compassion of verse 36 is a verb, splanchnizomai, formed from splanchna, the inward parts, the seat of strong feeling. It is rare in secular Greek and frequent in the Gospels, and in the synoptic Gospels it is used almost only of Jesus or of figures in His parables who stand for God, as in the father of the prodigal in Luke 15:20. Matthew uses it of Jesus here and in 14:14, 15:32 and 20:34. What He does follows what He feels each time.

The two words that describe the crowds, translated harassed and helpless, are eskulmenoi and errimmenoi. The first has the sense of being flayed, worried or bothered like a carcass torn by animals; the second has the sense of being thrown down, cast out or flung aside. They describe sheep that have been mauled and then abandoned. The image sharpens the charge of Ezekiel 34:4 and 34:5, that the flock was scattered and eaten.

Finally, in verse 38 the disciples are to ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers, and the verb is ekbalo, the very verb used for driving demons out in verse 33. It means to cast or thrust out. In the same chapter, the same verb describes the expulsion of a demon and the thrusting forth of labourers, and the disciples who pray will find that God answers by pushing them out the door.

typology.type: The sandwiched stories of the woman and the girl
typology.fulfillment: The ruler's daughter was twelve years old and the woman had suffered for twelve years. Twelve is the number of Israel's tribes, and the two daughters, one near death and one outcast, together picture a people both dying and unclean. Jesus restores them in the order the Gospel records, first the one who is cleaned by faith and then the one raised by His word. The unclean touch that should have made Him unclean makes her clean instead, a reversal of Leviticus 15:27, and the touch of a corpse that should have made Him unclean, Numbers 19:11, brings life. The pattern points to the greater work in which He takes uncleanness and death on Himself, 2 Corinthians 5:21, and gives purity and life. The type falls short because the girl will die again; the raising of Jesus Himself, Romans 6:9, is the one that does not.

typology.type: The Shepherd for sheep without a shepherd
typology.fulfillment: Moses prayed for a leader who would go out and come in before the people, Numbers 27:16-17, and Joshua, whose name is the Hebrew form of Jesus, was appointed, Numbers 27:18. Ezekiel 34:23 promised one shepherd, David, to feed the flock. In Matthew's story, Jesus is the leader Moses asked for and the shepherd Ezekiel promised, and He says so in John 10:11 when He calls Himself the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. The type falls short in that Joshua led a nation into a land; Jesus gathers those from every nation, John 10:16, and the Chief Shepherd will appear again, 1 Peter 5:4.

typology.type: The blind who see the King
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 35:5 promised that the eyes of the blind would be opened as a sign of the coming of God. The two men in verse 27 address Jesus as Son of David before any sight is given, so they see the identity of Jesus before their eyes are opened to anything else. Matthew keeps the motif: the blind will see again in 20:30-34, and in 12:23 it is the crowd that wonders whether He is the Son of David, while the Pharisees are the ones who cannot see. The type is fulfilled as physical sight and as spiritual sight, and Jesus uses the same pattern in John 9:39. It remains incomplete until the day the Lamb is on the throne and His people see His face, Revelation 22:4.

The prophets used harvest for the gathering of a scattered people, Isaiah 27:12, and for judgment, Joel 3:13. Jesus joins both senses to His own work, as the Lord of the harvest who will send reapers out, Matthew 13:39, and who at the end will send His angels to gather. The disciples are not the owners of the field; they are asked to pray and then to work in a field that belongs to another. The correspondence is with Israel's own harvest festivals, which were times of joy at God's provision, and the escalation is that the Lord of the harvest now gathers people for Himself, John 4:35-38. The harvest remains a picture, not a programme, and will only be finished at the end of the age.

study.christ:
This passage leads to Christ by showing Him in each office that Israel was awaiting. He is addressed as Son of David by two blind men, and Matthew has opened his gospel with the phrase in 1:1, so that the title is neither a stray compliment nor a casual hope. He is the heir of the promise given to David in 2 Samuel 7:12-16, and the one whose reign was to bring justice to the afflicted, Psalm 72:12-14. The men are the first in Matthew to use the title in the mouth of a petitioner, and they do it before they see anything, which fits the text of Romans 10:17, that faith comes from hearing.

He is also the shepherd of Ezekiel 34. The chapter lists what bad shepherds failed to do: strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind up the injured, bring back the strays and search for the lost. The four scenes of this passage perform that list. He heals the sick woman, brings back from death the daughter, restores the blind, and sets free the man silenced by a demon. The God who said, I will seek the lost, is here seeking them, and Matthew's readers are meant to see that the promise of Ezekiel 34:11 has an address. Jesus will later say plainly that He is the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11, and Matthew will quote Zechariah's picture of the shepherd who is struck and the flock scattered, Matthew 26:31. The compassion of verse 36 and the cross of chapter 27 are therefore the same love at different depths.

The passage leads to Christ by the pattern of touch. He lets a woman who is unclean touch Him, and takes a dead girl's hand. In the Law, contact with a discharge or a corpse spreads uncleanness, Leviticus 15:27 and Numbers 19:11. In Jesus the movement runs the other way: His wholeness spreads to what He touches. This is what the New Testament means when it says He took our infirmities, Matthew 8:17, and when it says that for our sake God made Him to be sin who knew no sin, 2 Corinthians 5:21. The girl's rising is a small sign of the resurrection of Jesus, who is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Corinthians 15:20.

Finally, He is the Lord who recruits. He does not ask the disciples to find their own harvest; He says to ask the Lord of the harvest. In John 4:35-38 He claims the field, and in Matthew 28:18-19 He sends out those who will go. The prayer of verse 38 is addressed to the Father, and the answer comes in the sending that Jesus Himself carries out in the next chapter.

A word of caution applies. The twelve years of the woman and the age of the girl are matched details, but Matthew does not make a doctrine of them, and the passage does not need an allegory of each coin or cloak. The links above rest on what Matthew and the other New Testament writers themselves say.
study.god:
The first thing this passage shows about God is that He feels. Verse 36 is bold: Jesus saw the crowds, and in His inward parts He was moved. Greek-speaking readers would have found it striking that the one who commands the winds and the dead is also the one whose gut turns at the sight of lost people. The Old Testament had said the same of God. In Hosea 11:8 His compassion grows warm and tender, and in Psalm 103:13 He has compassion as a father has for children. This passage tells us that this compassion is not a metaphor chosen for the Old Testament and abandoned in the New; it is on show in the face of the Son.

He is also the God who is addressed and who answers. The ruler asks, the woman reaches, the men cry out, and none of them is turned away. In each case, God incarnate responds to what is brought, whether a plain request, a whispered hope, or a shout in the street. Yet His answers do not look alike: a hand taken in a quiet room, a verdict spoken to a woman in a crowd, a question put to two men, a demon silenced without a word. He adapts the manner to the person, so that the one who heals is not a machine with a single mode. And in the question He asks the blind men, Do you believe that I am able to do this?, He treats the sufferers as persons whose trust matters.

God shows His authority over what people feared most. Death is a sleep, a demon is driven out, blindness and muteness end. What Israel's neighbours treated as the realm of rival powers is a realm over which He rules without strain. The Pharisees' charge, that this authority comes from the prince of demons, is a charge that evil can rival God, and Jesus will answer it in Matthew 12:25-29 by pointing out that a kingdom divided cannot stand and that a strong man must be bound before his house is plundered.

This God also holds sovereignty and prayer together. The harvest is His, and the Lord of the harvest is the one who sends. Yet the disciples are told to ask. The doctrine of God that emerges does not treat prayer as pointless because God already knows the need, nor as a way to move a reluctant God. It treats prayer as the means by which His people are drawn into the work He already intends, and by which the one who prays is changed from spectator to labourer.

For worship, this passage asks us to bring the whole range of need, as these people did, in whatever form it takes: bereavement, long illness, weak sight, silence. It also asks us to worship a God whose heart is not distant from the crowd. It is a comfort to the lonely and a rebuke to the cynical, that the Lord of heaven and earth looks at people who are harassed and helpless and does not look away.

crossReferences.note: Moses asks the LORD, the God of the spirits of all flesh, to appoint a man who will lead the people out and in, so that they will not be like sheep without a shepherd. Matthew 9:36 almost quotes this, and Jesus is the answer to a prayer as old as the wilderness. The Joshua of the next verse shares His name.

The charge against Israel's shepherds, that they did not strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind up the injured, bring back the strays or search for the lost. Each scene in Matthew 9 does what the failed shepherds left undone, so that the passage reads as the first answer to the lament.

The LORD promises that He will tend His flock, seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken and strengthen the weak. Matthew's miracles are presented as that promise being carried out in person, in the Messiah who has come among the sheep.

The law of the long discharge, which makes a woman unclean and her bed and seat unclean to others. It explains why the woman in verse 20 approaches from behind and in secret, and why it matters that touching Jesus does not leave Him defiled but leaves her clean.

The commandment of tassels on garments as a reminder to keep the Lord's commandments. The fringe the woman touches belongs to a garment that was meant to keep the law in sight, and she finds in its wearer the one who fulfils the law's purpose.

The parallel account of Jairus, which adds the Aramaic words Talitha koum, the messengers who say it is too late, and the command to believe. Reading it beside Matthew shows how Matthew compresses the story to keep its focus on the authority of Jesus and the faith of the two petitioners.

Jesus again calls death sleep, and the disciples misunderstand until He says plainly that Lazarus is dead. The passage shows that His sleep language is not a denial of death but a declaration about His power to undo it.

Two blind men again cry out, Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us, and this time the crowd tries to silence them. Matthew uses the pair to bracket the public ministry of Jesus, from the early Galilean miracles to the road to Jerusalem.

A near repetition of verses 32 to 34, with the mute man now also blind and the Pharisees' charge expanded by the name Beelzebul. What began as a murmur in chapter 9 grows to open warfare in chapter 12, where Jesus answers it directly.

Jesus tells His disciples to lift up their eyes and see fields ripe for harvest, and reminds them that they enter into labour that others began. It is the same harvest image seen from the field itself, and it shows that the shortage of workers is a matter of sight and willingness as well as number.

The sending of the seventy opens with nearly the same words as Matthew 9:37-38, which shows that Jesus said this more than once and made it a standing prayer. It also places the prayer before any plan, instructing the church to begin its mission on its knees.

Peter calls the elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not lording it over them, and promises a crown when the Chief Shepherd appears. It is the church's answer to Ezekiel 34, now asked to be the kind of shepherd its Lord is.

study.oneStory:
The Bible has been asking for a shepherd since the wilderness. When Moses was told he would not enter the land, his first concern was for the people who would be left, Numbers 27:15-17. When Israel's kings failed, the prophets said the flock was scattered and plundered, 1 Kings 22:17 and Ezekiel 34:5-6, and they pledged that the LORD Himself would come to find His sheep, Ezekiel 34:11. The wilderness prayer, the lament of the prophets and the promise of God are all gathered in the glance Jesus gives in Matthew 9:36. This passage is where the long waiting for a shepherd begins to be answered.

It also answers the older story of death. From Genesis 3 on, the human story is marked by a sentence that no one escapes, and by uncleanness that cuts people off. The woman and the girl represent both: a life that seeps away and a life that ends. When Jesus takes a dead hand and the child rises, the first small crack appears in that long sentence. It is only a sign, since the girl will one day die again, but it points to the day when the Shepherd Himself is struck and the sheep are scattered, Matthew 26:31, and then is raised, and so shows what the end will be, 1 Corinthians 15:20-26.

The passage sets up what follows. The harvest saying leads at once into chapter 10, and from there to the Great Commission, where the Lord of all authority sends His people to all nations, Matthew 28:18-20. The church in Acts begins with an answer to the prayer of verse 38, as the Spirit sets apart workers, Acts 13:2. Paul can say of this age that the work is plentiful and that God has given the ministry of reconciliation, 2 Corinthians 5:18.

The story ends where the shepherd image ends. In Revelation 7:17 the Lamb in the middle of the throne becomes the shepherd of the great multitude drawn from every nation, leading them to springs of living water, and God wipes every tear from their eyes. The crowds who were harassed and helpless become a multitude who are fed and led. The bleeding woman, the little girl and the blind men are the first of that harvest, brought in by a Shepherd who looked at them and was moved.

quiz.q: How was the woman with the twelve-year bleeding healed?

options.text: She touched Jesus' cloak in faith, and He told her that her faith had healed her.
options.note: Verses 20-22 show her faith reaching out, and Jesus crediting her healing to that faith.

options.text: Jesus laid His hands on her and prayed over her.
options.note: She touched Him; He did not lay hands on her here, though He affirmed her faith.

options.text: She was healed simply by being near the crowd.
options.note: It was her faith-filled touch of His cloak, not mere proximity, that Jesus commended.

options.text: She paid the physicians who finally cured her.
options.note: Physicians had not helped; her healing came through faith in Jesus.

quiz.q: What did Jesus say about the synagogue leader's dead daughter?

options.text: The girl is not dead but asleep, and He raised her by taking her hand.
options.note: Verses 24-25 show Jesus reframing death as sleep and raising the girl.

options.text: That nothing could be done because she had already died.
options.note: The opposite; He raised her, treating death as sleep, not as final.

options.text: That her death was a punishment for sin.
options.note: Jesus makes no such claim; He raises her, calling death sleep.

options.text: That she would be raised only at the last day.
options.note: He raised her then and there, not only at the final resurrection.

quiz.q: What did the two blind men call Jesus, and what does it signify?

options.text: Son of David, confessing Him as the promised Messiah of David's line.
options.note: Verse 27 has them hail Him with the royal messianic title.

options.text: Teacher, showing they respected His instruction.
options.note: They went further, calling Him Son of David, the messianic King, not merely a teacher.

options.text: Prophet, placing Him among the prophets of old.
options.note: They confessed Him as Son of David, a higher claim than prophet.

options.text: Friend, expressing their affection for Him.
options.note: They cried out to Him as the messianic Son of David, not merely a friend.

quiz.q: How did the crowds and the Pharisees differ in response to the freed mute man?

options.text: The crowds marveled, but the Pharisees said He cast out demons by the prince of demons.
options.note: Verses 33-34 contrast the crowds' amazement with the Pharisees' hardened charge.

options.text: Both the crowds and the Pharisees praised God together.
options.note: Only the crowds marveled; the Pharisees attributed the work to the prince of demons.

options.text: The crowds were afraid while the Pharisees believed.
options.note: The reverse; the crowds marveled and the Pharisees opposed Him.

options.text: Both dismissed the miracle as a trick.
options.note: The crowds were amazed and said nothing like it had been seen in Israel.

quiz.q: What moved Jesus as He saw the crowds, and what did He tell His disciples?

options.text: Compassion for harassed, shepherdless people, and to pray the Lord of the harvest for workers.
options.note: Verses 36-38 show His compassion and His call to pray for laborers.

options.text: Frustration at the crowds, and to send them away.
options.note: He felt deep compassion, not frustration, and called for workers rather than dismissing them.

options.text: Concern that the harvest was too small to bother with.
options.note: He said the harvest was plentiful, not small; the shortage was of workers.

options.text: A desire to rest, and to stop teaching the crowds.
options.note: He was moved to expand the mission, calling for workers, not to withdraw from it.

questions: The bleeding woman reached out in trembling faith and Jesus honored it. Where do you need to reach out to Jesus in faith, even if your faith feels small or hesitant?
Jesus treated the girl's death as sleep, showing His mastery over death. How does His power over death change the way you face loss, fear, and your own mortality?
The same works that amazed the crowds hardened the Pharisees. What keeps some hearts open and others closed to Jesus, and how is your own heart responding to Him?
Jesus was moved with gut-deep compassion for harassed and helpless crowds. Who around you is harassed and shepherdless, and how might Jesus want to move you with the same compassion?
Jesus commanded His disciples to pray for workers for the harvest. Will you pray that prayer this week, and are you open to being part of the answer?

translationNotes.note: The fringe of His cloak refers to the tassels an Israelite wore on the corners of his garment, Numbers 15:38-39; the woman's chronic bleeding made her ceremonially unclean, which explains her secret approach.
The prince of demons refers to Beelzebul, the charge Jesus will answer at length in Matthew 12:22-32.
Harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd echoes Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34, where God promises to shepherd His scattered flock Himself.
